text:
Keep the Joined-Up Hand

Every few years, someone in education declares that cursive is finished. Keyboards have won, the argument goes, and children should spend their scarce classroom hours on skills they will actually use. It is a tidy case, and it is wrong. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting, not out of nostalgia but because it serves children in ways that are practical, cognitive and social. The right question is not whether handwriting is old. It is whether a taught, fluent, joined script does something for a seven-year-old that other methods do not. I think it does.

Start with the most basic point: children still write by hand, and they will for a long time. Walk into any primary classroom and count the pencils. Spelling tests, maths working, story drafts, labels on science diagrams, notes passed to a teacher, and, in many countries, the written examinations that matter most at age eleven and beyond. Even in schools that are well stocked with tablets, the pen remains the everyday tool for most children. If handwriting is going to be used, it should be taught well. A child who has never been shown an efficient way to form letters will invent one, and the inventions are often poor: letters started from the bottom, awkward grips, constant lifting of the pencil, and a slow, effortful scrawl that tires the hand after two sentences. Teaching handwriting is not a luxury. It is the difference between a child who writes comfortably and one who dreads it.

The case for joining, specifically, rests on fluency. Printed letters require the writer to lift the pencil after every character, which breaks the movement into dozens of tiny stop-start motions per sentence. Joined writing lets the hand travel in rhythmic strokes, with whole words produced as a single motion. Done properly, this is faster and less tiring. It also builds a sense of the word as a unit rather than a string of separate letters, which has a plausible link to spelling. A child who writes "ing" or "tion" as a connected flow is rehearsing the pattern in the muscles as well as the eye. Teachers of dyslexic pupils have long observed that continuous cursive movement can help, because the motion of the hand reinforces the order of letters, and because there is no confusion between reversible shapes such as b and d when each begins with its own entry stroke. This is not a universal cure, and the research is not uniform, but the practical experience of many specialist teachers points the same way.

Then there is the evidence on what handwriting does to learning itself. Studies comparing handwriting with typing, including work using brain imaging, have repeatedly found that writing letters by hand engages the brain more richly than pressing keys. Children who practise forming letters by hand tend to recognise those letters better, and some studies suggest they compose longer and more fluent texts. Research on note-taking points in a similar direction: students writing by hand tend to process and summarise as they go, because they cannot keep up with speech word for word, while keyboard users often transcribe without thinking. Not every finding is as strong as headlines suggest, and the studies mostly compare handwriting in general with typing, not joined with print. But they establish the broad principle that the physical act of forming letters is not just a delivery mechanism for thought. It is part of how young children learn the written language. A curriculum that drops the careful teaching of that act is taking a risk with something that appears to matter.

The obvious objection is time. The primary day is crowded, and every minute of handwriting practice is a minute not spent on reading, number or science. This is a fair concern, but it points to a better solution than abolition. Handwriting instruction works best in short, frequent bursts, ten minutes a few times a week, folded into spelling and phonics work. The cost is small. The cost of not doing it is larger: children who cannot write fluently spend their working memory on forming letters rather than on what they want to say, and that taxes every subject. A child struggling to produce legible text will write less, and less carefully, in history and science as well as English. Fluent handwriting frees the mind for content. It is an investment that pays back across the whole curriculum, and the maths of time favours keeping it.

A second objection is that joined-up writing is just one style among many, and that print is simpler. Many schools now teach print first and join later, or skip joining entirely. I would argue for the opposite sequence in its spirit: teach letters with exit strokes from the start, so that joining grows naturally from the way the child already writes, rather than being bolted on at age seven as a separate, harder system to learn. Several well-regarded schemes do exactly this. The point is that the finished goal should be a legible, speedy, joined hand, not a permanent block-capital print that tops out at a modest speed. Print has its uses, and no one needs to ban it, but a child who leaves primary school writing only in disconnected letters has been given less than they could have had.

What about the claim that typing is the skill of the future? It is a real skill, and children should learn it. But the choice is a false one. Handwriting and keyboard fluency are not rivals competing for a single slot; they are complementary, and most children can learn both. The argument that we should drop handwriting because keyboards exist is like arguing that we should drop mental arithmetic because calculators exist. Both tools have their place, and the person who can use both is better equipped than the one who can use only one. There is also a plain practical point: devices run out of battery, schools have limited hardware, and exams are still handwritten in many systems. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly by hand is exposed in exactly the high-stakes moments where it counts most.

There is a cultural argument too, though it should not carry the weight of the case. Cursive is how people sign their names, read old letters, and decipher the handwriting in a grandparent's recipe book or a historical archive. A child who cannot read joined script is cut off from a large body of written material, including family documents. This is a modest reason, but it is a real one, and it costs nothing extra once the skill is taught. Equally, handwriting is personal. A hand-written note carries a trace of the writer in a way that typed text does not, and many children take quiet pride in developing a style of their own. That pride, and the care it encourages, is not nothing.

I should be fair about the limits of the case. The research is not conclusive on every point, and anyone who claims that cursive makes children cleverer is overselling. Some children, especially those with significant motor difficulties, will do better with adapted methods or with technology, and schools should provide them without stigma. Rigid insistence on a single approach, marked down for a slanted loop, would be silly. And there is no reason to teach handwriting badly: endless copying of pages, or grading neatness over content, turns a useful skill into a chore. The argument is for sensible, well-taught, modest-time handwriting instruction, not for a revival of the copybook.

But the burden of proof lies with those who want to remove something that has served children for centuries. They need to show that dropping joined writing will leave children better off, and the evidence does not show that. What it shows, at best, is that handwriting supports learning, that fluency matters, and that children who write easily write more. The cost of keeping joined-up writing is a few short lessons a week. The cost of abandoning it is uncertain, possibly large, and hard to reverse once a generation of teachers has lost the habit of teaching it.

So keep it. Teach children to form letters carefully, to join them smoothly, and to build a hand that is quick, clear and their own. Teach them to type as well. Give them both tools and let them choose what suits the task. A child who can do both is not held back by the past; she is simply better equipped for the present.
